title: Brown or Black Layers Inside an Onion: What It Means

seo.title: Brown or Black Layers Inside an Onion: Safe or Spoiled?
seo.meta_description: One dry brown internal layer can be localized damage and may be removed if neighboring layers are crisp. Black powdery growth, wet softness, slime, or decay across multiple layers is a reason to discard the onion.
seo.search_intent: Explain dry internal browning versus black mold and soft rot in onions and give trim-or-toss guidance.

excerpt: A single dry brown ring can be peeled away if the rest of the onion is firm. Black powdery mold, wet or slimy layers, bad odor, or widespread internal damage means the bulb should be discarded.
content_html:
Onions are layered, which means one scale can fail while the layers around it still look normal. You may cut through a good-looking bulb and find either a single dry brown ring or black material dusting several inner surfaces. Those findings are not equivalent. Color gets your attention, but moisture, texture, odor, and how far the change extends are what tell you whether the problem is localized.

A dry brown scale can be localized

Handling injury, dehydration, and storage disorders can discolor one layer. If it is dry and sharply defined and the next layers are crisp, peel it away and inspect the bulb. The remaining sound tissue can be used.

Remove the entire affected scale rather than scraping only the darkest spot. Then feel the next layer on both sides of the defect. If the onion immediately returns to crisp, juicy tissue with a normal smell, that supports the idea of a localized storage or handling problem rather than spreading decay.

Black powder can be fungal growth

UC Davis lists black mold caused by Aspergillus niger as an onion storage disease, with black discoloration and shriveling around the neck and scales. If black dusty growth has penetrated between multiple layers, especially with soft or wet tissue, do not treat it as a cosmetic ring.

A small dark mark on the dry papery skin is different from black dust that keeps reappearing as you peel fleshy layers. The farther it has traveled into the bulb, the less useful it is to keep chasing clean-looking rings one by one.

Moisture is the key warning sign

Dry discoloration is one thing. Brown or black layers that are water-soaked, slimy, mushy, or leaking point toward active breakdown. A sour or rotten odor reinforces that call.

Texture is often clearer than color. A dry damaged scale may tear or flake; a rotting scale can smear, collapse, or leave liquid on the knife. If wetness and softness extend across several layers, the onion has moved beyond the kind of defect that can be handled by peeling one dry ring away.

A practical cut-open guide

FindingWhat to do
One dry brown internal layerRemove and inspect neighboring scales
Dry bruise with firm tissue belowTrim generously
Black powder or fungal growth across layersDiscard if it has spread into the bulb
Wet, slimy, mushy, foul-smelling layersDiscard

If a defect looks limited, cut the onion in another direction to check whether it continues through the bulb. When similar damage shows up in several places, the overall pattern matters more than one patch that still looks usable.

What if the black material is only under the papery skin?

A little dark material confined to the dry outer skins does not automatically mean the fleshy layers are involved. Peel the onion over an easy-to-clean surface and inspect the first juicy scale. If it is crisp and clear, the situation may be limited.

If black powder keeps appearing on fleshy layers as you peel, the growth has penetrated farther. Avoid shaking a heavily moldy onion around other foods, discard it, and clean the cutting surface afterward. Wash your hands before moving on to produce that will be eaten raw.

Remove a bad onion from the bag quickly

If one onion in a mesh bag is wet, moldy, or leaking, take it out and inspect the neighbors. A decaying bulb can raise local moisture and soil the skins of nearby onions. Keeping the remaining onions dry and well ventilated is more useful than leaving the damaged one in place and hoping the problem stays isolated.

Pay special attention to the bases and necks of bulbs that were touching it. You do not need to throw away every firm, dry onion automatically, but separating them and using them sooner makes sense. A ventilated basket or mesh bag also makes it easier to spot a failing onion before it affects the storage environment around it.

Once you cut it, use it promptly

Refrigerate cut onion in a covered container. If you have already found an internal defect, cooking the sound portion that day is better than returning the opened bulb to the refrigerator for a long hold.

Knife and cutting-board hygiene matter too. If the blade passed through wet rot or mold, clean it before cutting tissue you plan to keep or before moving on to another food. Dry and isolated can be peeled away; wet, moldy, and spreading should not be chased layer by layer.

faq.question: Can I eat an onion with one brown layer inside?
faq.answer: Yes, when the layer is dry and isolated and the surrounding layers remain crisp, clean, and normal-smelling.

faq.question: What is black powder inside an onion?
faq.answer: It can be black mold, including Aspergillus niger. Widespread growth between layers is a reason to discard the bulb.

faq.question: What if the brown layer is wet?
faq.answer: Wet, slimy, or mushy discoloration is more concerning for breakdown or rot than a dry brown scale.
